title: Big Questions
description: Big Questions — philosophy for children through to young adults: wondering and asking good questions, fairness, friendship, what is real, what makes a good person, identity, how we know things, thought experiments, philosophers from India, China, Greece and beyond, mind and free will, ethical theories, justice, and the meaning of life. Lessons model respectful disagreement and reasoning, and present philosophical views as positions to examine, not answers to adopt.

lessons.title: Big Questions, Little Thinkers
objectives: Ask "why" and "what if" questions
Listen to and respond to others' ideas
explanation: Philosophy means "love of wisdom". Philosophers ask big questions that don't have easy answers, like "What is a friend?" or "Why do we dream?"
Everyone can be a philosopher — even children! When we wonder about something and ask "why?" or "what if?", we are doing philosophy.
In philosophy, we listen carefully to others, give reasons for our ideas ("I think... because...") and it's okay to change our minds.

story.title: The Question Jar
story.text: Ivaan's family kept a question jar. Every night, someone picked a question. Tonight Ivaan picked, "Can a fish be happy?" Papa said, "Maybe, if it's swimming freely." Aaji said, "How would we know?" Ivaan thought hard. "Maybe if it wiggles its tail fast!" Everyone laughed, and the conversation went on until bedtime.

lessons.title: Is It Fair?
objectives: Talk about whether situations are fair or unfair
Explain that fair doesn't always mean the same
explanation: Fairness is about treating people rightly. Sharing a cake into equal pieces seems fair.
But sometimes fair isn't exactly the same. If one friend can't reach a high shelf, giving them a step stool is fair, even if others don't get one. People have different needs.
When things feel unfair, we can talk about it kindly and try to find a better way together.

lessons.title: What Makes a Friend?
objectives: Explain what makes someone a friend
Discuss tricky friendship questions with reasons
explanation: A friend is someone you like and who likes you, who is kind, plays with you and helps you. But philosophers ask deeper questions: Can you be friends with someone you've never met? Can a pet be a friend?

The Greek philosopher Aristotle, over 2,300 years ago, said there are friendships of usefulness, of pleasure (fun) and the best kind — friendships of goodness, where friends care about each other for who they are.
Friends sometimes disagree or fall out. Saying sorry and listening can help make up.

lessons.title: Was It Just a Dream?
objectives: Discuss the difference between dreams, pretend and real
Give reasons for how we know something is real
explanation: When we dream, things can feel real — flying, talking animals — but when we wake up, we know it was a dream.
An old Chinese story tells of the philosopher Zhuangzi, who dreamed he was a butterfly. When he woke, he wondered: "Am I a man who dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming I am a man?"
How do we know what is real? We can check with our senses, ask others, or see if it stays the same over time. But philosophers find this question surprisingly hard!

lessons.title: The Ring of Invisibility
objectives: Discuss what makes a person good
Reflect on whether people are good only because they might be caught
explanation: Virtues are good qualities of character, like honesty, courage, kindness, patience and fairness. Many traditions — Greek, Indian, Chinese — have lists of virtues.
Plato, a Greek philosopher, told the story of the Ring of Gyges: a shepherd finds a ring that makes him invisible. Would people still be good if no one could see what they did?
Aristotle thought virtues are like skills: we become honest by practising honesty, brave by practising brave actions. Character grows with practice.

lessons.title: The Ship of Theseus
objectives: Discuss the Ship of Theseus puzzle
Reflect on what makes a person the same over time
explanation: You were once a baby. Your body has grown and changed, and you think differently. Are you still the same person?
An ancient Greek puzzle asks: the hero Theseus's ship was kept in a harbour. As old planks rotted, they were replaced one by one, until no original plank remained. Is it still the same ship?
Philosophers give different answers: some say memories make us the same person; some say our body; some say our character or story. In Buddhist thought, there is no fixed, unchanging self.

vocabulary.meaning: what makes something the same thing over time

story.text: Grandpa's bicycle was 50 years old. Over the years, he had replaced the tyres, the seat, the chain, the handlebars and even the frame. "Is it still your first bicycle?" Ivaan asked. Grandpa scratched his head. "The parts are new, but the memories are old." Ivaan thought: "Maybe that's what makes it the same bike."

revision.notes: Retrieval first, then review notes; interleave with other units; apply in a new example.

lessons.title: Knowledge, Belief and Opinion
objectives: Distinguish facts, beliefs and opinions
Evaluate sources of knowledge: senses, reasoning and testimony
explanation: A fact can be checked with evidence ("Water boils at 100 °C at sea level"). An opinion expresses personal preference ("Mango is the best fruit"). A belief is something a person holds to be true, which may or may not be supported by evidence.

Philosophers have long defined knowledge roughly as "justified true belief" — you believe it, it's true, and you have good reasons. In 1963, Edmund Gettier showed cases where all three hold, yet it still doesn't seem like knowledge, sparking much debate.
We gain knowledge through senses (which can be fooled by optical illusions), reasoning and testimony (learning from others). Indian philosophers called these pramanas — means of knowledge.

vocabulary.meaning: something that can be checked with evidence

examples: An optical illusion where equal lines look different.
Learning about Antarctica from books (testimony).

story.title: The Stopped Clock
story.text: Raj glanced at the hall clock: 3 o'clock. He believed it was 3 o'clock, and it actually was. But the clock had stopped exactly 24 hours earlier! He had a true belief with a reason — yet did he really know the time? His philosophy teacher smiled. "That's a Gettier-style puzzle. Philosophers are still arguing about it."

lessons.title: The Experience Machine
objectives: Explain what a thought experiment is
Analyse Nozick's experience machine and what it reveals about values
explanation: A thought experiment is an imagined scenario used to test ideas. You can't build it, but thinking it through reveals what we believe.

In 1974, philosopher Robert Nozick imagined an "experience machine" that could give you any experiences you wanted — feeling you'd written a great novel or made a friend — while you floated in a tank. Would you plug in for life? Many people say no, suggesting we value doing things and real connections, not just feeling good.
Other thought experiments ask: if a robot behaved exactly like a person, would it have feelings? Thought experiments don't give final answers but sharpen our thinking.

vocabulary.meaning: an imagined scenario used to test ideas

examples: Nozick's experience machine.
Imagining a robot with feelings.

story.title: The Happiness Tank
story.text: Meera's class discussed Nozick's machine. Raj said, "I'd plug in! I'd feel like a cricket champion every day." Meera disagreed: "But you wouldn't really be one. I want to actually earn it." Their teacher asked, "So what do you value — the feeling or the reality?" The debate went on all lunch.

lessons.title: Many Paths to Wisdom
objectives: Describe key ideas of philosophers from Greece, China and India
Compare their approaches to living well
explanation: In Athens, Socrates (c. 470–399 BCE) questioned people to expose unclear thinking — the Socratic method — and said "the unexamined life is not worth living". Plato and Aristotle built on his work.

In China, Confucius (551–479 BCE, traditional dates) taught ren (humaneness), ritual and good relationships in families and society. Laozi, traditionally the author of the Daodejing, taught living in harmony with the Dao (the Way).

In India, the classical darshanas (schools) include Nyaya (logic), Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa and Vedanta, along with Buddhist, Jain and Charvaka (materialist) philosophies. The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths about suffering and its end.
examples: Socrates questioning citizens in the marketplace.
The Charvaka school questioning life after death.

story.title: The Gadfly of Athens
story.text: Socrates called himself a gadfly, stinging Athens awake with questions. He asked generals what courage was and judges what justice was — and showed they couldn't define them. Some loved him; others were angry. In 399 BCE, he was sentenced to death. He chose to accept it rather than abandon philosophy.

lessons.title: Are We Free?
objectives: Explain the mind-body problem and the Turing test
Evaluate positions on free will and determinism
explanation: The mind-body problem asks how the mind (thoughts, feelings) relates to the body (brain). René Descartes (17th century) argued mind and body are different substances (dualism); many scientists and philosophers today think the mind arises from brain activity (physicalism). The debate continues.

In 1950, Alan Turing proposed a test: if a machine's conversation can't be distinguished from a human's, should we say it thinks? Critics like John Searle (the Chinese Room, 1980) argued that producing the right outputs isn't the same as understanding.

Free will: determinism says every event is caused by earlier events. If so, are our choices free? Compatibilists say freedom means acting on your own reasons without being forced; libertarians (in philosophy) say true freedom requires choices not fully determined; hard determinists say free will is an illusion.

vocabulary.meaning: the view that mind and body are separate
the view that all events are caused by prior events
the view that free will and determinism can both be true
awareness of oneself and the world

examples: Searle's Chinese Room thought experiment.
Choosing tea or coffee — free or determined?

story.title: The Chinese Room
story.text: Searle imagined himself in a room with a rulebook for matching Chinese symbols. People slip in questions in Chinese; he follows the rules and slips out perfect answers — without understanding a word. "That," he argued, "is what a computer does." Others replied that the whole system might understand. The argument still divides philosophers.

lessons.title: Three Ways to Think About Right and Wrong
objectives: Compare consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics
Apply ethical theories to real dilemmas
explanation: Consequentialism judges actions by their results. Utilitarianism (Jeremy Bentham, John Stuart Mill) aims for the greatest happiness for the greatest number. Critics say it can justify harming individuals for the majority.

Deontology, associated with Immanuel Kant, judges actions by duties and rules: some acts, like lying or using people merely as tools, are wrong regardless of results. Critics say rigid rules can lead to bad outcomes.

Virtue ethics (Aristotle, Confucius) asks what a good person would do, focusing on character. Indian traditions emphasise dharma and ahimsa (non-violence); Gandhi developed satyagraha — "truth-force" — as a method of non-violent resistance.

vocabulary.meaning: judging actions by duties and rules

examples: The trolley problem: diverting a runaway trolley to save five but harm one.
Gandhi's Salt March of 1930.

story.title: The Salt March
story.text: In 1930, Gandhi and 78 companions walked about 385 km to Dandi to make salt from seawater, breaking the British salt law non-violently. Thousands joined; tens of thousands were arrested. Gandhi argued that means and ends are inseparable — a just cause must be pursued by just methods. His ideas later inspired Martin Luther King Jr.

lessons.title: Justice and the Meaning of Life
objectives: Analyse Rawls's and Ambedkar's ideas of justice
Evaluate different answers to the question of life's meaning
explanation: In "A Theory of Justice" (1971), John Rawls proposed the "veil of ignorance": design society's rules without knowing whether you'll be rich or poor, of which caste, gender or ability. He argued people would choose equal basic liberties and allow inequalities only if they benefit the least advantaged.

Dr B. R. Ambedkar, chief architect of India's Constitution, argued that political democracy must rest on social democracy — liberty, equality and fraternity as a union. He fought caste discrimination, warning that political equality alongside social inequality was a contradiction.

What gives life meaning? Some find it in religious faith; existentialists like Albert Camus and Jean-Paul Sartre argued we create our own meaning; others point to relationships, contribution, knowledge or love. Philosophy helps us examine our answers, not just accept them.

vocabulary.meaning: imagining society's rules without knowing your place in it
a sense of shared brotherhood and sisterhood
a philosophy emphasising freedom and creating meaning

examples: Designing school rules without knowing which student you'd be.

story.title: A Life of Contradictions
story.text: On 25 November 1949, Dr Ambedkar warned the Constituent Assembly: "On the 26th of January 1950, we are going to enter into a life of contradictions. In politics we will have equality and in social and economic life we will have inequality." He urged the nation to remove this contradiction as soon as possible — a challenge still discussed today.
